correctness.rationale: A nonempty feasible bundle occupies one part; if goods remain, maximality requires every bundle to be nonempty and every used part to be completely colored. Unit EF1 is exactly a class-size spread of at most one. If m≤n, singleton assignment is complete; if the largest part has at least n items, dividing that entire part evenly works. Otherwise choose the first prefix that reaches n, with previous sum B<n and last part size t≤a1. The sum of lower class quotas is B−Σ_{before last}⌊a_i/2⌋+⌈t/2⌉≤B+1≤n, while the upper quotas sum to at least n. Integer quotas totaling n therefore exist and each used part splits into exactly that many singletons and pairs. B+t≤2n−2; at m=n the bound also holds under a1<n (thus n≥2). The claimed time is valid by scanning explicit part lists, sorting r sizes, and writing the bundles. In K_{3,3,3}, a complete equitable split among four classes requires sizes 3,2,2,2, but each three-item part would need a class of size three. Two split parts do give a maximal partial coloring. Independent bounded replay checked 9,570 graph/agent instances via a direct search for pair quotas, including unsorted part lists and n=1.
residual_risks: The finite replay does not prove arbitrary sizes; the quota inequality does.
The complexity is for the construction on part lists, not a benchmark of the uploaded finite checker (which recomputes prefix sums in its input preparation).

value.rationale: The result solves the maximal equitable partial coloring problem for a natural unrestricted family beyond trees and includes cases where complete equity is impossible. It yields an explicit efficient construction and a bound on the number of colored goods in a nontrivial regime. The motivating four-agent K_{3,3,3} case separates the task from a mere application of a complete coloring theorem.
residual_risks: The theorem assumes unit values; it does not promise to optimize the number of assigned goods or generalize to nonuniform weights or general graphs.
